extracted.intended_audience: general news readers and viewers interested in media criticism (Fox News audience)
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion column evaluating a high-profile anchor's credibility and how a network should handle false reporting, using the Brian Williams controversy as a case study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stop the bleeding: get the facts out
rubrics_metrics.description: The first rule when you make a mistake, especially one of this magnitude, is to stop the bleeding by getting the facts out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt, transparent disclosure of facts is the appropriate initial response to a major journalistic error; failing to do so (as Williams apparently did) prompts more criticism and prolongs the controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness / 'Do not lie' (cardinal rule of journalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: He broke the cardinal rule of journalism: he lied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honesty is the fundamental journalistic standard; knowingly reporting false personal accounts undermines credibility and can justify calls for removal or discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency from the network (avoid 'no-comment' posture)
rubrics_metrics.description: NBC’s no-comment stance just reinforces the notion that the network wants the controversy to magically disappear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A network's refusal to address a controversy can appear evasive and worsen public perception; proactive engagement and explanation are preferable to silence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal accountability regardless of stature
rubrics_metrics.description: If an NBC correspondent had told such a false story on air, he or she would be lucky to get off with a reprimand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational discipline should be applied consistently — high-profile 'bankable' anchors should not receive unduly lenient treatment simply because of their status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration and factual verification with eyewitnesses/sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Stars & Stripes ... contradicts this account; flight engineers and other veterans provided alternative accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims, especially first-person battlefield stories, should be corroborated with primary sources and records; discrepancies between an anchor's account and eyewitness reports are decisive in assessing truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid embellishment; maintain consistency in personal accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Williams accurately reported his first-person story ... but over the years repeatedly told the false version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and anchors should avoid embellishing personal narratives; repeated retellings that alter key facts degrade credibility and invite scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology clarity and factual alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: In his 'Nightly News' apology, Williams said he was 'instead on a following aircraft,' and he wrote on Facebook that 'I was indeed on the Chinook behind the bird that took the RPG.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apologies should be precise and aligned with verifiable facts; ambiguous or later-contradicted apologies will not restore trust and may intensify criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider stakeholder sensitivity (e.g., veterans)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The last group of people he wants to offend are veterans, and that’s ... stinging him the most.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When journalistic errors implicate specific communities (like veterans), sensitivity to their reactions matters both morally and for reputational repair; offending key constituencies increases reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism / overreaching reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather overreached in trying to report a sensational story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chasing sensational angles or overreaching in reporting increases risk of error; heavy verification and cautious framing are needed when claims are potentially sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational calculus: reputational capital influences consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When it comes to the NBC franchise, Brian Williams is too big to fail. He’s the face of the network ... He’s a bankable asset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media organizations weigh an individual's value and track record when deciding consequences; being a top-rated, bankable figure can mitigate disciplinary actions even after serious credibility lapses.
